content: The Logan School for Creative Learning is a private educational institution located in Denver, Colorado. It caters specifically to intellectually gifted students from kindergarten through eighth grade. The school employs experiential learning as its primary educational methodology. The institution was established in 1989 under the name The Denver School by Patricia McKinnell, who was one of the founding teachers and currently serves as the Dean of Students. Initially, the school operated out of a garage. Since 1999, the Logan School has been situated on the former Lowry Air Force Base, a 1,866-acre site that is being redeveloped into a mixed-use urban community. The school is one of several independent schools located on this site. The mission of the Logan School is to provide a challenging educational environment tailored to gifted children aged four to fourteen. The school is also associated with the Edward E. Ford Fellowship for Aspiring School Heads, a year-long leadership development program supported by the National Association of Independent Schools and the Edward E. Ford Foundation. The curriculum at the Logan School is specifically designed for intellectually gifted students aged four to fourteen. Admission is determined through a combination of test scores, a student visit, and teacher recommendations. Each student receives an individualized curriculum that is tailored to their unique abilities, learning styles, and personal interests. At the start of each academic year, students select a unit of study, with older students often choosing more than one. These units are based on the students' interests, as they will dedicate a significant portion of their school time to studying these topics. The unit-based curriculum integrates subjects such as reading, writing, mathematics, and science, fostering connections between these disciplines and the students' chosen areas of interest. Field trips are a vital component of the program, often emphasizing environmental themes. The school comprises 12 core classrooms, with students grouped by age, typically within a two-year range. Students usually remain with the same teacher for two years and address their teachers by their first names. During the 1998-1999 school year, one class at Logan participated in a research project investigating the usability of perspectives-based software for collaborative learning. This project was part of their studies on acid mine drainage from old gold mines in Colorado. Some students from the Logan School have received recognition for their work, including an award from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL). During the 2005-2006 school year, the Logan School conducted a fundraising initiative called The Logan Legacy Campaign, which successfully raised over $5 million to support the school's expansion. This effort was led by the Head of School, Andrew Slater. Prior to the expansion, the school utilized only half of its main building, leaving the remaining portion unfinished and referred to as the Unoccupied Space. Following the expansion, this area was renovated, and classrooms were added throughout the building. The school now features a layout resembling a square horseshoe on the first level and a square on the second level. Behind the west side of the school lies a large berm, beyond which is a wetlands area. This location is a favored site for conducting environmental studies and enjoying the natural surroundings.
